The Department of Unused Time occupied the narrowest building on Bellwether Street. From the pavement it looked like a filing cabinet someone had forgotten to push shut.

Mara found it on a Tuesday, between a dentist’s appointment that ended early and a train that never came.

There was a brass plate beside the door.

**HOURS RETURNED, SUBJECT TO AVAILABILITY.**

Underneath, in smaller letters:

**Please do not bring clocks. They become difficult.**

She put her watch in her coat pocket, which seemed close enough, and went inside.

The waiting room contained three chairs, a fern, and a man holding a birthday cake. Its candles had burned down to blue puddles.

“Have you been waiting long?” Mara asked.

“That’s what I’m here to find out.”

Before she could decide whether he was joking, a woman behind the counter called her forward.

The woman wore a green cardigan with wooden buttons. On her desk stood a glass of water, a stapler, and a small stone labeled **THURSDAY**.

“What sort of time have you lost?”

“I’m not sure.”

“Most people aren’t. We can search by circumstance.”

Mara considered.

“Queues. Meetings. Trying to remember passwords.”

The woman nodded without writing anything.

“And there were eight years with someone who said he wasn’t ready.”

“We get that a lot. Unfortunately, time spent hoping is classified as used.”

“That seems unfair.”

“You can appeal.”

“Does it take long?”

The woman looked at her.

“Right,” Mara said.

A trolley rattled somewhere behind the wall.

“What can you return?”

“Small things, usually. Minutes misplaced between tasks. Afternoons you failed to notice. Occasionally a summer, though there’s a considerable backlog.”

Mara thought of her mother’s kitchen.

It had been demolished three years earlier, after the house was sold. The new owners sent photographs of the renovation, believing she would be pleased. White cabinets. Black taps. The wall where her mother had marked her height was gone.

“I’d like an hour with my mother.”

The woman’s expression changed only slightly.

“We can’t return people.”

“I know.”

“People often say that before asking.”

Mara looked down at the counter. Someone had scratched a tiny boat into its varnish.

“I didn’t mean—”

“I know.”

For a while, the woman searched through drawers. They were much deeper than the desk should have allowed. Mara heard wind in one and cutlery in another. From a third came the noise of children being told to come inside.

Finally, the woman placed a brown envelope on the counter.

“Forty-three minutes.”

“What are they from?”

“A Sunday in November. You were seventeen. You declined to help make bread.”

“I don’t remember that.”

“No.”

Mara touched the envelope. It was warm.

“If I open it, will I be there?”

“You’ll be here. The time will be yours again.”

“And my mother?”

“No.”

“Then what good is it?”

The woman drew the envelope back toward herself.

“I can put it away.”

Mara kept one finger on the corner.

“How much?”

“There’s no charge. But you must use it before midnight.”

***

At home, she put the envelope on the kitchen table.

She answered two emails. She washed a mug that was already clean. She called her brother and asked whether he remembered their mother making bread.

“She was terrible at it,” he said.

“She wasn’t.”

“Mara. You could build a garage with those loaves.”

She laughed, then cried so suddenly that he stopped speaking.

After a moment he said, “Are you all right?”

“Yes.”

“Want me to come over?”

“No. Thank you. No.”

When they hung up, she opened the cupboard.

Flour. Salt. A sachet of yeast far beyond its printed date.

She went to the corner shop.

By the time she returned, it was raining. She took off her wet shoes, cleared the table, and tore open the envelope.

Nothing shone.

There was no music, no kitchen rising around her, no familiar voice from the next room.

Inside was a square of ordinary paper.

**Begin.**

Mara nearly threw it away.

Instead, she found a recipe.

She tipped flour into a bowl. Added salt. Mixed the yeast with water that was probably too hot, then started again.

Dough stuck to her hands.

She had forgotten that part, or never known it: how thoroughly a thing could resist becoming itself.

She worked it against the table. Folded, pressed, turned. Rain clicked against the window.

Her mother had worn her rings while cooking. Bits of dough would lodge beneath the settings, and she would pick them out with a pin afterward. Mara had found this disgusting at seventeen.

She took off her own ring and set it beside the bowl.

For a moment she wanted to call her brother again. Then the dough caught under her palm, and she turned back to it.

***

The loaf came out crooked and pale on one side.

Mara cut it too soon. The middle dragged against the knife.

She buttered a slice anyway and ate it standing at the counter.

Outside, a bus sighed at the stop. Upstairs, someone dropped something heavy and swore. Her phone lit up with a message from her brother.

**Any good?**

She sent him a photograph.

Three dots appeared.

**Garage material?**

**Garden wall, at most.**

She wrapped half the loaf in a clean towel for him.

The next morning, Bellwether Street contained a dentist, a florist, and a narrow passage between two buildings.

Mara stood at the passage for a while. At the far end were bins and a delivery bicycle chained to a pipe.

She checked her watch. She had twenty minutes before work.

Across the street, the bakery was opening. She went in and asked the woman arranging the window why a loaf might come out pale on one side.

“Your oven, probably. What shelf did you use?”

Mara explained.

The woman listened, then moved two chairs away from a little table.

“Sit down,” she said. “I’ve got a minute.”
